ethiopia.title: ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - ENA English
ethiopia.content: ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us ENDF at 119: Advancing Ethiopia’s Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance 🔇Unmute By Staff Writer October 25, 2026 (ENA) The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), marking 119 years of institutional development, represents a longstanding pillar of Ethiopia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national security. From defending the country’s independence to participating in international peacekeeping operations and expanding domestic defense manufacturing, the institution has continued to evolve in response to changing national, regional and global security demands. Today, the ENDF is pursuing a transformation that extends beyond conventional military strength. Reforms in organizational structure, professional training, technological development and defense production are intended to strengthen its operational capabilities and reduce dependence on external suppliers. At the same time, its contributions to peace and security at national, regional and international levels remain important dimensions of its institutional responsibilities. The development of the force reflects the relationship between national defense, institutional resilience and technological capacity. Its future effectiveness will depend not only on the equipment it possesses, but also on the professionalism of its personnel, the strength of its institutions and its ability to contribute to lasting peace. Resilience Legacy Ethiopia’s military history is closely connected with its struggle to preserve independence and territorial integrity. Across successive generations, the country’s armed forces have defended national sovereignty while adapting to changing political circumstances, military doctrines and technological developments. The ENDF’s historical legacy includes the wider tradition of Ethiopian resistance to colonial aggression, notably the victory at Adwa in 1896, as well as the military experiences that shaped the country’s subsequent defense institutions. These historical milestones preceded the establishment of the modern army and helped shape the national consciousness surrounding sovereignty and independence. Over the decades, the armed forces have undergone changes in command structures, training systems, equipment and operational responsibilities. The contemporary ENDF is building on this historical experience while seeking to develop a more professional, technologically capable and institutionally resilient force. The reform agenda pursued in recent years places particular emphasis on organizational unity, operational readiness, specialized capabilities and modern military science. In July 2026, ENDF Chief of Staff Field Marshal Birhanu Jula said the force had strengthened its unity, expanded its organizational structure and continued modernizing its equipment and technology amid an increasingly complex security environment. These efforts, he said, were intended to reinforce its capacity to safeguard Ethiopia’s sovereignty. The significance of this transformation lies in its effort to connect historical experience with the requirements of contemporary national defense. A modern military must combine discipline and institutional continuity with scientific knowledge, technical expertise and the capacity to respond to rapidly changing security conditions. A Pillar of National Peace The ENDF’s principal constitutional responsibility is to defend Ethiopia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Its contribution to national peace also involves protecting the country against armed threats, responding to security emergencies and supporting conditions in which citizens can pursue their social and economic activities in safety. National peace, however, extends beyond military operations. Sustainable stability requires functioning institutions, political dialogue, reconciliation, respect for the law and public confidence. The defense force can contribute to these objectives by maintaining professionalism, observing constitutional responsibilities and protecting civilians in accordance with applicable law. The ENDF’s experience in complex security environments has reinforced the importance of coordination, intelligence, training and operational preparedness. Its ongoing institutional reforms seek to strengthen these capabilities while adapting to emerging threats. The force’s relationship with the public is equally important. National defense is most effective when the military operates as a professional institution serving the country and its people, rather than a particular political interest. Maintaining political neutrality, respecting civilian authority and upholding the rights of citizens are essential to sustaining public trust. The military’s role in national peace should therefore be assessed not only through its ability to confront armed threats, but also through its adherence to the law, protection of civilians and contribution to an environment conducive to reconciliation and development. In a country with diverse communities and complex social and political dynamics, lasting peace requires cooperation among security institutions, public authorities, communities and other stakeholders. The ENDF’s professional conduct and institutional accountability are important to this broader national effort. Regional Security Ethiopia occupies a strategically important position in the Horn of Africa, a region where security developments frequently cross-national borders. The ENDF’s contribution to regional peace includes cooperation with neighboring countries and participation in regional security mechanisms. Ethiopia has maintained an important role in the Eastern Africa Standby Force, an African regional arrangement designed to support peace operations and respond to crises. In May 2026, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula reaffirmed Ethiopia’s commitment to regional peace and security during discussions with the outgoing and incoming leadership of the Eastern Africa Standby Force. The meeting highlighted the importance of regional cooperation in addressing shared security challenges. Such cooperation demonstrates that national defense and regional stability are interconnected. Information sharing, military coordination, joint preparedness and professional exchanges can help countries respond more effectively to threats that no single state can address independently. The ENDF’s regional responsibilities must also be understood within the broader principle that durable security cannot be achieved through military measures alone. Diplomatic engagement, peaceful settlement of disputes, economic cooperation and respect for national sovereignty remain essential to preventing conflicts and strengthening relations among neighboring countries. A stable Horn of Africa would create greater opportunities for regional trade, infrastructure development, investment and economic integration. By contributing to legitimate regional security arrangements and supporting cooperative approaches to shared threats, Ethiopia’s defense institutions can help create conditions for these wider development objectives. International Peacekeeping One of the most visible expressions of Ethiopia’s contribution to international peace has been its participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. Ethiopian personnel have served in international missions for decades, reflecting the country’s longstanding engagement with multilateral efforts to maintain peace and protect communities affected by conflict. According to the United Nations, Ethiopia’s participation in UN-authorized operations dates back to 1951, when Ethiopian personnel served as part of the multinational force in the Korean War. Since then, Ethiopian military personnel have contributed to peace and security operations in different parts of the world. A prominent example is the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA), established in 2011 to help stabilize the disputed Abyei area between Sudan and South Sudan. The mission monitors security arrangements, supports the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, and contributes to efforts to prevent renewed violence. The deployment of Ethiopian troops to Abyei followed an agreement reached by Sudanese and South Sudanese representatives in Addis Ababa. The mission illustrates how Ethiopian military personnel have supported internationally mandated security arrangements in a sensitive border region. Ethiopian personnel have also served in other United Nations missions, including operations in South Sudan. Their responsibilities have included supporting civilian protection, maintaining security in designated areas and helping create conditions for humanitarian activities and political processes. These experiences have given Ethiopian peacekeepers opportunities to work within multinational command structures, cooperate with personnel from different countries and apply international peacekeeping standards in demanding operational environments. International peacekeeping also strengthens professional experience. Service in multinational missions exposes military personnel to different approaches to logistics, communication, civilian protection and operational coordination. Lessons gained from these assignments can contribute to training and institutional development at home. The broader significance of Ethiopia’s peacekeeping record is that military capability can serve purposes beyond national defense. When deployed under an authorized mandate and in accordance with international law, disciplined military personnel can help protect vulnerable populations, support humanitarian access and contribute to efforts to restore stability. Defense Technology, Industrial Capacity Alongside its peace and security responsibilities, the ENDF is pursuing a transformation in military technology and domestic production. The objective is to strengthen the country’s ability to manufacture, maintain and sustain essential defense equipment while developing the technical expertise required for modern military operations. For a country with extensive security responsibilities, dependence on foreign suppliers can affect the availability, maintenance and long-term sustainability of military equipment. Developing domestic production capacity can help reduce these vulnerabilities, retain technical knowledge and build a stronger industrial foundation for national defense. Ethiopia’s defense industrial institutions provide important examples of this approach. The Homicho Ammunition Engineering Complex is associated with domestic ammunition production, while the wider defense industry has been working to strengthen capabilities in equipment manufacturing, engineering and maintenance. These facilities illustrate how defense production can bring together mechanical engineering, industrial processes, technical training and specialized manufacturing. Their strategic importance lies not simply in the products they manufacture, but also in the knowledge and skills developed through sustained industrial activity. Developing domestic expertise in this field can also expand opportunities for engineering research and technical education. Another significant step came in June 2026, when the Information Network Security Administration and the Ethiopian Air Force signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a drone technology center and strengthen research, laboratory cooperation and aerospace capabilities. The initiative is intended to support innovation and the development of local expertise in unmanned aerial systems. In August 2026, the ENDF and the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute also signed a cooperation agreement to explore the application of artificial intelligence in areas including logistics, military training, cybersecurity, military healthcare, air operations and electronic warfare. The agreement points to a broader shift in defense modernization. Military effectiveness increasingly depends on the ability to collect, process and use information, maintain secure communications and support rapid, informed decision-making. Artificial intelligence and related digital technologies could contribute to these objectives, although their operational benefits will depend on research, testing, qualified personnel and effective implementation. These initiatives demonstrate that Ethiopia’s defense transformation is not limited to acquiring modern equipment. It also involves building the scientific, industrial and educational capabilities required to develop and sustain advanced systems. Human Capital Dimension Technology alone cannot create an effective defense institution. Modern military systems require skilled operators, engineers, technicians, researchers, maintenance specialists and commanders capable of applying scientific knowledge to operational requirements. For this reason, investment in military education and professional development is central to the ENDF’s modernization. Military academies, specialized training institutions and cooperation with civilian research organizations can help develop the expertise needed to operate sophisticated equipment and maintain complex systems. The partnership between the ENDF, the Ethiopian Air Force, the Information Network Security Administration and the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute illustrates the potential value of cooperation between defense institutions and the wider scientific community. Such partnerships can strengthen research capacity, encourage the exchange of technical knowledge and support the development of locally relevant solutions. They can also help cultivate a generation of Ethiopian engineers and researchers whose expertise may contribute to defense manufacturing and other technology-intensive sectors. Domestic defense production can generate benefits beyond the military when it develops transferable industrial skills, strengthens engineering capacity and encourages research and innovation. The long-term objective is to build a system in which training, research, manufacturing and operational requirements reinforce one another. This would enable Ethiopia to develop more of the expertise necessary to maintain its defense capabilities while creating a stronger foundation for technological advancement. Self-Reliance The ENDF’s industrial and technological transformation forms part of Ethiopia’s wider pursuit of productive capacity and economic self-reliance. Similar priorities are evident in the country’s efforts to expand agricultural production, develop mineral resources, strengthen manufacturing and invest in scientific knowledge. Defense production has a distinct purpose because it is directly connected to national security. Nevertheless, it can contribute to broader industrial development by encouraging specialized engineering, technical training and domestic manufacturing. The development of ammunition production, engineering facilities and drone research demonstrates the range of capabilities required to build a more self-reliant defense sector. These initiatives can help strengthen maintenance capacity, improve the availability of selected equipment and create opportunities for domestic technical expertise. It is important, however, to distinguish progress in selected areas from complete self-sufficiency. Modern military systems depend on extensive supply chains involving specialized components, software, materials and technical knowledge. Building sustainable domestic capacity is therefore a continuing process that requires investment, research, reliable production standards and international technical cooperation where necessary. The strongest measure of progress is not the number of factories established or the equipment acquired, but the ability to produce reliable systems, maintain them over time, develop skilled personnel and meet clearly identified national defense requirements. A more capable domestic defense industry can strengthen strategic autonomy by giving Ethiopia greater control over parts of its supply chains. It can also improve the country’s capacity to respond to changing security requirements without relying exclusively on external procurement. The Road Ahead As the ENDF marks 119 years of institutional development, its future will be shaped by its ability to combine historical experience with professional standards, technological innovation and a commitment to peace. Its responsibilities remain broad: protecting national sovereignty, contributing to domestic security within the law, supporting regional stability and participating in international peacekeeping. Meeting these responsibilities requires an institution that is well trained, technically capable, disciplined and accountable. The development of domestic defense industries, drone technology and artificial intelligence cooperation indicates a growing emphasis on technological preparedness. Sustaining these efforts will require stronger research institutions, skilled human resources, effective industrial management and continued adaptation to changing military technologies. Equally important is the relationship between security and peace. Military readiness can deter threats and help protect communities, but lasting stability also depends on dialogue, diplomacy, reconciliation and cooperation among nations and communities. The ENDF’s long-term contribution will be strengthened when professional defense capabilities complement these wider efforts. The force’s 119-year institutional journey thus represents both a historical legacy and a continuing responsibility. Its achievements in national defense, regional cooperation, international peacekeeping and technological development provide a foundation on which further progress can be built. Ultimately, the strength of the Ethiopian National Defense Force will be measured not only by its capacity to defend the country, but also by its professionalism, its contribution to a secure regional environment and its ability to adapt responsibly to the demands of modern defense. By combining institutional resilience with technological advancement and a sustained commitment to peace, the ENDF can continue to serve as an important pillar of Ethiopia’s sovereignty and national development. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) recently celebrated its 119th anniversary, highlighting its crucial role in safeguarding Ethiopia's sovereignty and contributing to regional stability. The ENDF has evolved significantly, focusing on reforms in organizational structure, professional training, and technological advancements to enhance its operational capabilities and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. Its historical legacy, rooted in the defense of national independence, informs its current transformation towards a more professional and technologically adept military. The ENDF's responsibilities extend beyond military operations to include promoting national peace through civilian protection and institutional accountability. Additionally, the force plays a vital role in regional security cooperation and international peacekeeping, participating in UN missions since 1951. Recent initiatives aim to bolster Ethiopia's defense technology and domestic production capabilities, exemplified by the establishment of a drone technology center. These efforts are designed to ensure sustainable national defense while fostering regional cooperation and economic development.

Password recovery Recover your password your email A password will be e-mailed to you. borkena Ethiopian News and Opinion Home Featured Latest News Business Opinion Video Amharic Entertainment Restaurant Travel Sport Books Blog Business Listings Jobs Support Us Contact Sign in / Join Wednesday, October 28, 2026 Facebook Linkedin Telegram TikTok WhatsApp Instagram X Youtube Home News Kore Zone Declares Security Crisis Amid West Guji Border Raids News October 27, 2026 Updated: October 27, 2026 Kore Zone Declares Security Crisis Amid West Guji Border Raids October 27, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Local officials warn regional security forces are overwhelmed as cross-border incursions leave communities vulnerable and infrastructure paralyzed By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — Local administrative structures in the Kore Zone of the South Ethiopia Region have declared themselves incapable of protecting civilian populations, stating that ongoing cross-border raids and property looting by armed groups from the West Guji Zone in Oromia have overwhelmed regional security forces. Zonal and woreda officials confirmed that recurrent armed incursions between October 22 and 24, 2026, targeted several kebeles, including Jalo, Kore, and Shafula. The latest attacks resulted in four fatalities and five severe injuries, including a father and child as well as children aged seven to ten. On October 26, local residents held joint funerals for victims in Kore Kebele, while officials separately verified that a 14-year-old child and two household heads were killed in Jerlo Kebele. Over the past week alone, armed groups operating across the regional boundary have killed four civilians in Kore, injured three others, and stolen over 100 head of livestock, following similar attacks against agrarian communities in the neighboring Burji Zone. Addressing the deteriorating situation, Gorka Woreda Administrator Melkamu Asfaw stated that the armed incursions are identity-based and ethnically targeted. Melkamu emphasized that the absence of federal security units leaves local communities vulnerable, noting that woreda authorities lack the operational capacity to safeguard their populations. Local security sources and regional administrators affirmed that while regional special strike forces deploy to contested border points, the scale of the insurgency exceeds regional capacities, necessitating direct federal intervention to restore stability. The security collapse along the Oromia–South Ethiopia boundary has severely disrupted commercial transit and vital infrastructure. Residents reported that the main arterial highway connecting Kore Zone to Dilla has remained closed for 11 years due to lingering security threats, forcing commercial transport to reroute through Arba Minch. Demonstrating the ongoing danger along transport corridors, an Isuzu commercial truck driver was shot and killed on the route on October 26. Officials and bereaved families noted that regional police routinely arrive long after attackers retreat across the zonal border, leaving border communities trapped in chronic insecurity and displacement. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Ethiopian Sports News Join the conversation. These incursions, which occurred between October 22 and 24, 2026, have overwhelmed regional security forces, leaving communities vulnerable and infrastructure paralyzed. Reports indicate that the attacks resulted in four deaths and multiple injuries, including children. Local authorities have highlighted the identity-based nature of these assaults and the lack of federal security presence, which exacerbates the situation. The ongoing violence has disrupted vital commercial routes, with the main highway to Dilla closed for 11 years due to security threats. Residents have expressed frustration over delayed responses from regional police, who often arrive after attackers have retreated. The situation calls for urgent federal intervention to restore stability and protect the affected communities.

ethiopia.title: Peace-Security Anchor Ethiopia Must Consolidate Commitments to Peace and Security: Former PM - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Peace-Security Anchor Ethiopia Must Consolidate Commitments to Peace and Security: Former PM - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Peace-Security Anchor Ethiopia Must Consolidate Commitments to Peace and Security: Former PM - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Peace-Security Anchor Ethiopia Must Consolidate Commitments to Peace and Security: Former PM 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 27, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia, which remains an anchor for peace and security in the region, must strengthen and continue this genuine commitment to peace, former Ethiopian Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn told ENA. Speaking to ENA on the sidelines of the recent 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, he noted that the country remains an anchor for peace and security in the region. The diplomatic efforts made when the Sudan crisis arose and the ongoing shared role it continues to play in Somalia are examples in this regard, Hailemariam said, stressing that Ethiopia must greatly strengthen and continue this genuine commitment to peace. According to him, there also is a commendable effort for a peace agenda to exist and for peace to come within the country as well. "When we look at all these things broadly, Ethiopia has continued to be an anchor state; and it must continue to do so," the former premier underscored. Commenting on the High-Level Forum, he highlighted the platform's success in fostering open and unvarnished dialogue among African leaders on pressing regional security challenges. Hailemariam emphasized that the Tana Forum sets itself apart from standard international gatherings by prioritizing candid exchange over political posture. “What distinguishes the Tana Forum from other well-known platforms is that it is a platform that allows people to speak their minds and express what they truly feel,” he explained. “Elsewhere, there is what is called a diplomatic language. The situation is often such that you pass through the middle without effectively conveying the message you want. So we needed a platform different from that; and we have come this far.” According to him, the Forum has played a vital, constructive role by delivering actionable recommendations and directly preparing comprehensive peace and security reports for the African Union over the past 12 years. In Ethiopia, there are also commendable ongoing efforts to ensure lasting peace within the country itself. Pointing to Ethiopia’s population of over 130 million, Hailemariam stressed that both domestic and regional stability directly impact the nation. He pointed out that the government's recent calls for peace reflect a practical commitment to resolving differences through open dialogue, negotiation, and a spirit of compromise rather than avoiding underlying issues. As peace benefits all, the former Prime Minister encouraged the continuous strengthening of peace initiatives to achieve tangible results across the region. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: Former Ethiopian Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn emphasized the importance of Ethiopia's role as a peace and security anchor in the region during the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa. He urged the country to strengthen its commitment to peace, highlighting Ethiopia's diplomatic efforts during the Sudan crisis and its ongoing involvement in Somalia as key examples. Hailemariam praised the Tana Forum for fostering open dialogue among African leaders, distinguishing it from other international platforms by encouraging candid discussions on pressing security challenges. He noted that the Forum has successfully provided actionable recommendations to the African Union over the past 12 years. Additionally, he pointed out Ethiopia's internal peace initiatives, stressing that both domestic and regional stability are crucial for the nation’s well-being. Hailemariam called for continued efforts in peacebuilding, advocating for dialogue and compromise to address underlying issues and achieve lasting peace across the region.

Opinion October 27, 2026 Updated: October 27, 2026 What can we learn about ethnic politics from the causes and consequences of the current Moyale conflict? October 27, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber By Yihenew Ewnetu Sweden Introduction The protracted land disputes and violent conflicts in the Moyale district of southern Ethiopia represent a profound case study in the history, demography, and politics of the Horn of Africa. Specifically, Moyale exemplifies the use of borderland communities (BLCs) as political tools and serves as a stark illustration of the destructive potential of ethnic politics and ethnic federalism. The recurring clashes between the indigenous Borana (Oromo) and Somali communities are not merely localized resource disputes; they are the direct result of a century of foreign colonial disruption and the calculated political maneuvering of successive Ethiopian regimes. The institutionalization of ethnic federalism in 1991 by the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) fundamentally transformed these historical tensions into systemic, permanent, zero-sum territorial warfare. This dynamic demonstrates how regimes routinely sacrifice peace and societal coexistence to secure demographic hegemony and political survival (Tache & Oba, 2009, p. 410). Under the current dominant and expansionist posture assumed by the Oromo Prosperity Party (PP) at both the regional and national levels, the conflict has grown significantly more complex and deadly. Historical Roots of the Moyale Conflict The foundational roots of the Moyale conflict trace back to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Historically, the Borana exercised dominant customary control over the vast rangelands spanning southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya. However, toward the end of the nineteenth century, Somali-affiliated groups, notably the Garri, initiated a westward expansion into the easternmost Borana grazing territories (Bassi, 2018, p. 112). Early twentieth-century British-Ethiopian border surveys, such as those conducted by Zaphiro, definitively recognized the Borana as the primary indigenous inhabitants of critical water-rich areas like Qadaduma, documenting that the Garri utilized these resources primarily as clients during seasonal dry periods. This dynamic shifted dramatically under Italian colonial occupation. The Italian authorities implemented a strict “divide and rule” strategy, systematically favoring Islamic and Somali-speaking groups to undermine the central Ethiopian state (Bassi, 2018, p. 114). Through extensive colonial armament, the Garri were empowered to militarily challenge Borana customary governance, successfully capturing critical eastern Dirre pastoral resources and vital dry-season water points like Eel Deer (Bassi, 2018, p. 115). Following the defeat of the Italians, local Garri leadership actively negotiated with Ethiopian and British transitional authorities to legitimize their retention of these newly acquired territories. By the 1960s, under Emperor Haile Selassie, these diplomatic frictions deteriorated into full-scale armed proxy conflicts driven by the geopolitical shockwaves of Somali irredentism. Garri factions shifted allegiances to fight under the banner of Somali nationalism, supporting the invading Barre regime’s territorial pushes into the Sidamo and Bale provinces. This culminated in severe regional clashes in 1969, during which Ethiopian Borana militias played a decisive military role in repelling Mogadishu-allied guerrilla advances (Bassi, 2018, p. 117; Tache & Oba, 2009, p. 415). Subsequently, the Derg regime (1974–1991) introduced an era of authoritarian centralization that temporarily suppressed the overt politicization of ethnic borders. The Derg delineated internal administrative boundaries based strictly on natural geographic features rather than ethno-linguistic identities (Engidashet & Shiferaw, 2023, p. 5). Under this rigid administrative framework, the Moyale district was administered exclusively within the Borana Awraja (Province). This allowed the Borana to maintain relatively uncontested administrative control over their traditional wells and rangelands (Bassi, 2018, p. 118). While localized resource conflicts persisted, they were managed through indigenous mechanisms, preventing escalation into formal territorial disputes until the Derg’s collapse in 1991 (Engidashet & Shiferaw, 2023, p. 6; Tache & Oba, 2009, p. 416). The EPRDF Era: Transnational Repression and Demographic Engineering (1991–2018) The fall of the Derg in 1991 unsealed these historical conflicts, coinciding directly with the rise of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and EPRDF regime led by Meles Zenawi. The political trajectory of Meles and the TPLF was deeply intertwined with the Somali Republic under Siad Barre. During the armed struggle, the TPLF and the Somali state shared a mutual enemy in the Derg. This strategic alignment led the TPLF to openly endorse and benefit from the Somali invasion of Ethiopia during the 1977–1978 Ogaden War (Tareke, 2009, p. 250). In return for this support, Barre’s government provided Meles Zenawi with political favors, including a luxury bungalow in Mogadishu, diplomatic and economic assistance, and a Somali state passport used to travel internationally and build vital networks (Clapham, 1998, p. 7). Upon assuming state control, Meles leveraged these historical ties to Somali factions to neutralize political opposition. Following the collapse of Siad Barre’s government, massive influxes of displaced populations—including former military officers, security operatives, and active allies of Barre’s previous invasions of Sidamo and Bale—flooded into northern Kenyan refugee camps such as Walda, Sololo, and Isiolo (Oromia Support Group, 1997, p. 8). Meles deployed these armed Somali factions, many personally known to him, as proxy squads to systematically harass, extort, and assassinate Ethiopian dissidents who had sought refuge in Kenya. The security situation in these camps rapidly deteriorated. Refugees and aid workers faced constant threats from armed bandits (shiftas), local militias, and cross-border incursions (Wagacha & Guiney, 2008, p. 16). A 1993 Human Rights Watch report noted that in January 1993 alone, 53 bandit attacks in Kenyan refugee camps resulted in the deaths of 38 refugees and 9 security personnel (Human Rights Watch, 1993, p. 18). Operating under the military direction of the Southern Command led by Hayelom Araya, EPRDF intelligence operatives functioned as assassination squads in Nairobi and border towns. The Kenyan government largely responded with diplomatic appeasement. This complicity peaked on July 2, 1992, when Ethiopian operatives assassinated the renowned Borana politician and former provincial governor, Jatani (Janani) Ali, in Nairobi. Under intense diplomatic pressure from Meles Zenawi’s government, Kenyan authorities quietly released the apprehended assassins without trial, triggering massive riots by the Ethiopian diaspora in Nairobi (Oromia Support Group, 1997, p. 5). This assassination campaign continued with the killing of Afewerki Asegid, a former official from Tigray province, within a UNHCR refugee camp in Thika. The extreme insecurity in camps like Walda and Isiolo forced the UNHCR to relocate refugees to the malaria-infested Kakuma and Dadaab camps (O’Sullivan, 2026, p. 538). Walda camp was officially closed in March 1993 (Wagacha & Guiney, 2008, p. 17). The relocation to Kakuma had severe health implications for Ethiopian refugees, evidenced by a staggering malaria incidence rate of 936 per 1,000 children at the time (World Scientific Public Health Compendium, 2002, p. 54). Simultaneously, to secure the southern borderlands from armed political opponents, the Meles administration utilized UNHCR resources to enact a massive campaign of demographic engineering. Between 1991 and 1993, the federal government officially resettled tens of thousands of Somalis from Kenyan camps directly into the contested Moyale district. This included transferring 44,294 people from the Walda refugee camp alongside an additional 35,000 Garri individuals registered at the Banissa camp (UNHCR, 1992, pp. 12-15; Bassi, 2018, p. 119). Borana leaders vehemently protested, demonstrating that these resettled populations were effectively Somali nationals or political operatives tied to the fallen Siad Barre regime with no prior history of residence, land ownership, or property in the Moyale area (Bassi, 2018, p. 119; Oromia Support Group, 1997, p. 8). Through this calculated political maneuver, the regime successfully grafted a heavily armed, loyalist demographic into southern Ethiopia, deliberately diluting the political dominance of the indigenous Borana community who had historically defended the southern part of the country. The state deliberately traded local stability for central control, proving that in the calculus of ethnic politics, peaceful coexistence is entirely expendable if it secures a geopolitical advantage (Tache & Oba, 2009, p. 418). This southern demographic engineering mirrored parallel TPLF strategies in the Amhara territories of Wolkait (Welkait) and Humera. In northern Ethiopia, the TPLF systematically weaponized refugee repatriation and demobilization programs to alter ethnic compositions and secure political hegemony. Between 1985 and 1987, the Relief Society of Tigray (REST) coordinated the return of an estimated 154,000 to 170,000 Tigrayan refugees from Sudan (Hendrie, 1996, p. 35). Instead of returning them to their arid regions of origin in central Tigray, the TPLF redirected them into the fertile, newly annexed Amhara territories of Wolkait, Humera, Dansha, and Tselemt (World Bank, 1993, p. 42). This shift was augmented by relocating 25,000 to 30,000 demobilized combatants and over 100,000 internal settlers, alongside 15,000 to 20,000 Tigrayans previously settled in the southwest (Young, 1997, p. 145). This engineered influx, coupled with the violent displacement of the indigenous Amhara populace, achieved a rapid demographic “tipping point.” By the 1994 census, the population of Humera, Wolkait, and Tsegede was recorded as 92.2% Tigrayan and a mere 6.3% Amhara (Central Statistical Agency, 1996, p. 12; Kassaw & Veneranda, 2024, Section 1). In both the north and the south, the EPRDF successfully co-opted international humanitarian frameworks to subsidize its ethno-political gerrymandering. The UNHCR served as the primary logistical and financial vehicle through its Special Emergency Programmes, while the World Bank provided critical post-civil war development funds meant for integrating redundant ex-combatants into civilian life (World Bank, 1993, p. 42). Instead, the TPLF utilized these international resources to finance massive settler-colonial projects, embedding ethnic federalism through federally funded demographic erasure. Administrative Demarcation and the 2004 Referendum It is true that there have always been Somali communities adjacent to the Borana Oromos. The fact that tens of thousands of Somalis were resettled in the area doesn’t mean that they were the only Somalis in the area. However the massive resettlements of the 1990s ensured that the geographic area of Moyale could no longer be governed by a single, unified local administration. The TPLF/EPRDF did not intend for its resettlement to create political balance, but rather to construct permanent conflict as a built-in feature of the ethnic federal system, ultimately making the Somali Regional State inherit the problem created by the demographic engineering project. Under the ethnic federalism system, the town and its surrounding pastoral lands were violently bifurcated: the Oromia Regional State administers its own Moyale district (woreda) under the Borena Zone, while the Somali Regional State administers a parallel Moyale district under the Liben (now Dawa) Zone. In October 2004, the federal government conducted a highly controversial referendum across the 1,400-kilometer Oromia-Somali border. Officially, the results overwhelmingly favored Oromia, with the National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) awarding the Oromia Regional State administrative control of roughly 80% of the contested kebeles, leaving 20% to the Somali Regional State (Kefale, 2010, p. 621). The Somali regional government and local clan elders outright rejected the results, accusing the Oromo People’s Democratic Organization (OPDO) of utilizing federal military backing, voter intimidation, and prior demographic manipulation to secure the outcome (Bassi, 2010, p. 238). Because the results were fiercely contested, local militias refused to vacate territories, rendering the referendum a paper exercise and transforming traditional resource competition into zero-sum border warfare (Tache & Oba, 2009, p. 420). The long-term impact of the demographic engineering was mirrored in the 2007 census. Projecting the baseline resettled population using Ethiopia’s national average population growth rate of 2.6%, the 80,000 resettled Somalis would grow to approximately 118,158 individuals over a 15-year period. This combined impact of initial mass resettlement and subsequent natural population growth was ultimately codified in the 2007 Census. The census recorded a massive population disparity reflecting this demographic shift: 254,137 residents in the Somali-administered Moyale district compared to only 31,162 in the adjacent Oromia-administered district (Central Statistical Agency of Ethiopia, 2010). The Escalation of Violence Under the Oromo-PP (Post-2018) Following the political transition in 2018, the Oromo political elite—led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed—assumed an expansionist posture of absolute dominance at both national and regional levels. This consolidation of power by the Oromo Prosperity Party (PP) structurally emboldened Oromo nationalists, regional paramilitaries, and local vigilante groups to violently reclaim administrative and territorial hegemony in Moyale (Engidashet & Shiferaw, 2023, p. 12). Prior to 2018, violence in the area was largely characterized by sporadic, albeit deadly, clashes between local militias utilizing light arms. However, the Oromo-PP’s consolidation of power and expansionist posture militarized the dispute to an unprecedented level. The conflict transformed into state-sponsored urban warfare, drawing in heavily armed Oromo regional paramilitaries acting as ethnic armies. The introduction of heavy weaponry, coordinated military offensives, and the full involvement of the Oromia regional state apparatuses meant that local disputes over flags or municipal boundaries could immediately trigger massive civilian casualties and systematic arson. The silence of the Oromo-led PP government regarding the conflict, and its tacit approval of the heavy-handedness of Oromo paramilitaries, continues to be the source of death and displacement for tens of thousands of residents. Consequently, citizens have lost hope and can no longer rely on the federal state for protection (Human Rights Watch, 2019, p. 45; Bayu, 2021, p. 28). The catastrophic escalation in October 2026 perfectly illustrates this dynamic. The immediate catalyst was an administrative and territorial dispute triggered by the opening of a new administrative office and the hoisting of a Somali Regional State flag in a contested area on October 18, 2026 (Borkena, 2026, p. 1). The raising of the flag sparked immediate resistance and protests by Oromo groups, resulting in the fatal shooting of a 13-year-old girl (Horn of Africa News, 2026, p. 1). While local elders and security representatives temporarily negotiated the lowering of the flag, counter-protests by Somali residents in Kebele 02 rapidly deteriorated into full-scale urban combat by October 21 (Reuters, 2026, p. 1). Rather than acting as a neutral arbiter, the state apparatus under the Oromo-PP routinely utilized regional and local forces to project muscle. Heavily armed Oromia regional special forces, operating alongside local Oromo vigilante militias, launched heavy offensives into Somali-inhabited districts. They engaged in intense, sustained gun battles with Somali regional security forces and local Somali combatants who were fiercely defending the demographic and administrative footholds they had secured through federal intervention in the 1990s (Capital FM, 2026, p. 1). The atrocities and socio-economic devastation from these politically engineered clashes have been severe. According to hospital officials cited by international media, the late October 2026 fighting left at least nine people dead and over 30 injured by heavy weapons (Reuters, 2026, p. 1). The violence featured the targeted torching of buildings, the suspension of critical cross-border transport to Nairobi and Addis Ababa, and the total paralysis of commercial activities. Unable to rely on the Ethiopian state for protection, tens of thousands of civilians—predominantly women and children—were forced to flee across the border into Marsabit County, Kenya, entering through points such as Sessi, Kore, Biashara, Foundation, and Miti (Capital FM, 2026, p. 1). This massive refugee influx prompted immediate Kenyan troop movements and heightened police surveillance along the border to secure Kenyan territory against militia spillover, while the Kenya Red Cross scrambled to provide emergency relief to the displaced populations (Pulse Kenya, 2026, p. 1). The Politicization of Borders and Permanentization of Conflict The protracted violence in the Moyale district serves as a tragic and profound case-in-point of how political greed, ethnic politics, and ethnic federalism can fundamentally destroy the organic coexistence of societies. The Ethiopian state’s approach to the southern BLCs illuminates a dark reality: regimes will readily sacrifice the long-term good and security of their citizens to secure their own political survival and demographic hegemony. The introduction of ethnic federalism by the EPRDF in 1991, later codified in the 1995 Constitution, weaponized these newly engineered demographics. Ethnic federalism inextricably linked land ownership, political representation, regional budgets, and resource access directly to ethnic identity (Kefale, 2010, p. 616). In doing so, the system politicized every local administrative border, transforming fluid, pastoral zones of interaction into rigid, militarized frontiers. Furthermore, ethnic politics ensures that the central government operates as a partisan entity. It does not matter whether a cunning minority ethnic regime like the TPLF—which ensures its political survival through satellite ethnic organizations—or an ethnocratic dictatorial regime like the Oromo-PP, which claims a majority base, controls the central government. Such governments are inherently partisan to their power base. Under ethnic federalism, d
ethiopia.summary: The ongoing conflict in Moyale, southern Ethiopia, highlights the complexities of ethnic politics and the consequences of historical land disputes. The clashes between the Borana (Oromo) and Somali communities stem from a century of colonial disruption and the strategic manipulation of ethnic identities by successive Ethiopian regimes. The establishment of ethnic federalism in 1991 by the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) exacerbated these tensions, transforming historical grievances into systemic territorial conflicts. The conflict's roots trace back to the late 19th century, when Somali groups began encroaching on Borana lands, a situation worsened by colonial policies that favored certain ethnic groups. The EPRDF's demographic engineering, including the resettlement of Somali populations into contested areas, aimed to dilute Borana political power, demonstrating how regimes prioritize control over peace. This situation underscores the destructive potential of ethnic federalism and the sacrifices made for political survival, revealing the intricate relationship between ethnicity and governance in Ethiopia.

The move comes amid growing use of mobile wallets, virtual cards and contactless payments, alongside concerns about cybercrime and financial fraud. According to the National Bank of Ethiopia, fraud losses totaled Birr 1.3 billion in 2024. Attempted cyberattacks against public and private institutions also rose by 115 percent during the first half of 2024 compared with the corresponding period in 2023. Mastercard's AI-powered systems can assess transaction risks within milliseconds, helping identify suspicious activity while reducing unnecessary declines of legitimate payments. In March 2026, the company introduced a transaction specific AI foundation model trained on hundreds of millions of anonymized transactions. The technology is designed to recognize complex fraud patterns that conventional detection systems may miss. The company is also promoting tokenization, which replaces actual card numbers with secure digital identifiers during transactions. By limiting exposure of sensitive payment information, the technology helps protect customers using online stores, digital wallets and contactless terminals. These measures complement Ethiopia's efforts to modernize its financial infrastructure, improve payment interoperability and reduce dependence on cash. Mastercard's local partnerships include initiatives with Dashen Bank and Ethiopian Airlines, such as the ShebaMiles Premium Cards, which offer travel benefits and international payment functionality. ethiopia.summary: Mastercard has announced the introduction of advanced AI and tokenization technologies to bolster digital payment security in Ethiopia. This initiative aims to enhance the safety and efficiency of online transactions, addressing the growing concerns over digital fraud and cyber threats. By implementing tokenization, Mastercard will replace sensitive payment information with unique identification symbols, ensuring that actual card details are not exposed during transactions. This move is part of Mastercard's broader strategy to support the digital economy in Ethiopia, which is experiencing rapid growth in e-commerce and mobile payments. The company emphasizes that these innovations will not only protect consumers but also foster trust in digital payment systems, encouraging more users to engage in online financial activities. Mastercard's efforts align with the Ethiopian government's goals to promote financial inclusion and digital transformation across the country.

somalia.content: Somalia opens fourth national cybersecurity forum as digital security efforts expand - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia opens fourth national cybersecurity forum as digital security efforts expand Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 27, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government opened its fourth National Cyber Security Forum on Tuesday in Mogadishu as the country expands efforts to protect its growing digital infrastructure. The two-day forum, organized by the National Communications Authority (NCA) and Mogadishu University, is being held under the theme “Building Trust and Cyber Resilience Through Security by Design.” advertisements The forum focuses on cybersecurity governance, protecting digital infrastructure, addressing emerging threats and strengthening national incident response capabilities. It also emphasizes integrating security measures into digital systems from the outset rather than introducing them after deployment. “Cybersecurity is a shared responsibility that requires collaboration among government, academia, private sector, and society,” Mogadishu University President Ibrahim Mohamed Mursal said. “Universities have an important role in developing the skills and research needed to address emerging cybersecurity issues.” Mursal also highlighted the university’s establishment of a new Department of Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence. Mr. Mustafa Yasin Sheikh, Director General of the NCA, highlighted key cybersecurity achievements, including the launch of the Somali Computer Incident Response Team (SOMCIRT), capacity-building programs for government officials, public awareness initiatives, and the development of cybersecurity risk and compliance management frameworks. “The progress we have made this year provides an important foundation for strengthening cybersecurity in Somalia. This forum offers an opportunity to share knowledge, research and expertise, and develop practical solutions to advance our national cybersecurity efforts,” he said. SOMCIRT was inaugurated on March 7 as Somalia’s first national center dedicated to coordinating the prevention, detection and response to cyber incidents. It operates under the communications authority and is responsible for receiving incident reports, issuing alerts and coordinating responses to threats affecting government institutions and critical infrastructure. The communications authority also completed its first cybersecurity certification program for government officials this year, training information technology professionals from 21 public institutions in internationally recognized cybersecurity standards and practices. Communications and Technology Minister Mohamed Adan Mo’allin who officially opened Tuesday’s forum said the government also plans to establish a National Cybersecurity Academy. “I hope this forum will produce practical outcomes that benefit the Somali people,” he said. Somalia has accelerated efforts to build a national cybersecurity framework as government services, telecommunications, banking and other sectors increasingly rely on digital systems. The House of the People approved a cybersecurity law in January establishing responsibilities for government agencies, critical infrastructure operators and national incident reporting and response. The law also formally provides for SOMCIRT. The National Cyber Security Forum was first held in Mogadishu in 2023. Previous editions have brought together public and private-sector institutions to discuss cyber threats, policy development, information sharing and protection of critical infrastructure. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Somalia president cancels Russia trip amid security, political pressures Somalia president cancels Russia trip amid security, political pressures October 28, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has canceled a planned trip to Russia this week because of mounting security and political pressures at home, the Somali Stream reported on Tuesday. The decision followed an ambush by Al Shabaab in Somalia’s Lower Shabelle region on Monday that killed dozens of Somali soldiers. Uganda presses Mohamud on opposition talks Uganda, a leading troop contributor to the African Union force in Somalia, has also pressed Mohamud to open talks with the opposition quickly or face the withdrawal of its troops. Mohamud made a one-day visit to Uganda this week and met President Yoweri Museveni. He asked Kampala to keep its forces in Somalia under a bilateral agreement, but Museveni declined, citing economic constraints. Museveni also urged Mohamud to engage the opposition and warned that Uganda would pull out all its troops if the advice went unheeded, leaving Mogadishu at risk of an Al-Shabaab takeover of the entire country. Mohamud calls for dialogue On Sunday night, before leaving for Kampala on Monday, Mohamud called for dialogue with the opposition and dropped his earlier refusal to compromise on the most contentious issues. The shift appeared aimed at placating Museveni. Since returning home, Mohamud has sought to ease political tensions and settle disputes across the country through political means, according to the Somali Stream. This decision follows a deadly ambush by Al Shabaab in the Lower Shabelle region, which resulted in the deaths of numerous Somali soldiers. Additionally, Uganda, a key contributor to the African Union forces in Somalia, has urged Mohamud to initiate talks with the opposition to avoid troop withdrawal. His recent actions reflect a strategic move to address both internal security challenges and external diplomatic pressures.

somalia.title: UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Diyar Guldogan Tuesday October 27, 2026 'This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,’ says spokesman The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on Oct. 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday. In a statement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said the mission would cease operations in accordance with Security Council resolutions and a request from Somalia’s federal government. advertisements “This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,” Dujarric said. The closure follows a jointly agreed transition roadmap under which UNTMIS’s mandated responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, funds and programmes. Guterres reaffirmed that the UN would continue supporting Somalia through its resident agencies and programmes, working with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners to promote peace, stability, human rights and sustainable development, Dujarric said. “Recognizing the significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges that remain, the Secretary-General calls for sustained international support to consolidate progress, advance inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions, and promote and protect human rights,” he added. Dujarric stressed that Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to the people of Somalia and to supporting Somali-led efforts to build a peaceful, stable and prosperous future. somalia.summary: The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its operations on October 31, marking the end of over three decades of UN involvement in the country. This decision follows a two-year transition period and aligns with requests from Somalia's federal government and Security Council resolutions. UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric emphasized that this milestone signifies the transfer of UNTMIS responsibilities to Somali institutions and various UN agencies. Despite the mission's closure, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres assured continued support for Somalia through resident agencies, focusing on peace, stability, human rights, and sustainable development. He highlighted the ongoing political, security, and humanitarian challenges in the country, calling for sustained international support to foster political dialogue, reconciliation, and institutional strengthening. Guterres reaffirmed the UN's commitment to aiding Somalia in its efforts to achieve a peaceful and prosperous future.

somalia.summary: Fighting in Somalia's South West State is escalating tensions between Kenya and Somalia, posing risks to regional security and trade, particularly affecting the miraa (khat) trade. Somali officials have accused Kenya of harboring Somali terrorists who allegedly plan to destabilize Somalia while receiving protection in Nairobi. This situation has led to increased diplomatic strain, as Somalia's parliament speaker has called on the federal government to confront Kenya about its perceived support for these militants. The ongoing conflict not only threatens the stability of Somalia but also jeopardizes the livelihoods of miraa traders in Kenya, who rely on the export of this cash crop to Somalia. As the violence continues, concerns grow over the implications for both countries' security and economic interests, highlighting the interconnectedness of regional dynamics in the Horn of Africa.

somalia.title: Trump mocks Somalia's airports in fresh Omar attack - Breakingthenews.net
somalia.summary: In a recent rally, former President Donald Trump targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, mocking her home country of Somalia by making disparaging remarks about its airports. Trump’s comments came as part of a broader critique of Omar, who has been a frequent target of his attacks due to her progressive policies and outspoken criticism of his administration. The remarks drew a mixed response, with some supporters cheering while others condemned the comments as xenophobic. Omar, who has faced similar rhetoric in the past, responded by emphasizing the importance of unity and respect for all communities. This incident highlights the ongoing tensions in American politics, particularly surrounding issues of race and immigration, as Trump continues to leverage controversial statements to energize his base ahead of the upcoming elections. The exchange underscores the polarized nature of political discourse in the U.S. and the challenges faced by minority representatives in Congress.

somalia.title: What Ilhan Omar’s Memoir Reveals About Her Date of Birth, Family History - Newsweek

The Minnesota Democrat's 2020 memoir, This Is What America Looks Like: My Journey From Refugee to Congresswoman, describes a childhood disrupted by fighting in Mogadishu and a journey that took the family through Somalia and Kenya before they were eventually resettled in the United States. Omar has faced a wave of scrutiny from MAGA hard-liners and conservative critics over longstanding, unproven allegations concerning her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Omar has repeatedly denied that Elmi is her brother or that their marriage was fraudulent. Federal agents searched Omar's Washington home on October 12, and investigators obtained a DNA sample, a source close to the matter previously told Newsweek. Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, also voluntarily spoke with investigators, according to the source. No court has found Omar committed immigration fraud. The memoir mentions Ahmed Abdisalan Hirsi, Omar's first husband, several times, but Elmi, whom Omar legally married in 2009, is not mentioned in Chapter 11, which covers 2009 to 2011. Omar has repeatedly rejected allegations about Elmi. In 2019, The Daily Beast reported the claim could be traced to an anonymous 2016 post on the Somali diaspora forum Somali Spot that provided no evidence and was written by a user the outlet said had a history of trolling. In her memoir, Omar says the scrutiny prompted her to issue a statement explaining her civil and religious marriages and separations. She says in her memoir she later regretted responding and describes the immigration fraud allegation, repeated by President Donald Trump in 2019, as a “baseless conspiracy theory.” What the Memoir Says About Omar's Age National Review senior political correspondent Jim Geraghty questioned Omar's birth date in a post on X, pointing to a chapter of her memoir headed "War: 1989-1991, Mogadishu, Somalia." Omar writes: "I was eight years old when civil war broke out in Somalia." Geraghty cited the July 1989 Mogadishu riots and argued that if Omar was eight at that point, she would have been born in 1981 rather than 1982. However, later in the same chapter, Omar describes 1992 as "the year after the war began," placing the war's beginning in 1991. That is consistent with her publicly listed birth date of October 4, 1982, which meant she was eight for most of 1991. "Representative Omar and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight," a section about Omar reads. "She spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before emigrating to the United States." The exact start of Somalia's civil war is not straightforward. The U.N.'s history of the conflict says Siad Barre fell in January 1991, while MSF's account describes Somalia as being in civil war by December 1990. The July 1989 riots occurred earlier, but the memoir does not say those riots were what Omar meant when she wrote that she was 8 when civil war broke out. In her memoir, Omar writes that she stopped wearing the hijab at 16, before returning to it at 23 and wearing it ever since. In a subsequent chapter, Omar describes herself as a "twenty-year-old mom” while pursuing an associate degree and says she later became pregnant again with her eldest child, Isra Hirsi, who was born on February 22, 2003, when Omar was 20. Will Chamberlain, senior counsel at the Article III Project and Internet Accountability Project, questioned Omar's birth date on X, pointing to her statement in the memoir that "I was thirty years old” and her account of a three-month trip to Africa in 2011. Chamberlain argued this would place her birth in 1981 at the latest. However, the chapter covers 2011-2012, and the two statements are separate: Omar says she was 30 while discussing completing her studies and elsewhere writes, “in 2011 I embarked on a three-month trip with my father.” In a February 13, 2014, Minnesota Star Tribune op-ed, Omar described herself as a “31-year-old Somali-Muslim woman, a mother of three and an unapologetic progressive.” The age is consistent with her listed birth date. The passage is also reproduced in her memoir. "Some suggest that as a woman, I meddle in political affairs and need to be 'put in my place,'" Omar wrote in the op-ed detailing an attack during a Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party caucus earlier that month resulting in her being treated for a concussion. "Some say I deserved what I got because my opinions are contrary to those of a few male political leaders in our community. In addition, a small group has decided that one Somali elected official is enough and now the community should sit down and be quiet." Omar's office did not return inquiries by Newsweek on Tuesday related to her memoir. The Family's Move to the United States Omar writes that her family discussed resettling in the United States while living in the Utange refugee camp in Kenya. She initially opposed leaving, telling her family, "I don't want to go anywhere!" Her father told her, "The United States is different," and said America could become their home. The family then went through the refugee resettlement process. During an interview with a UNHCR official, Omar writes that officials took the names and birth dates of every family member. Her father and four oldest siblings were questioned, while the three youngest sat to the side. The family learned about a year later that they had passed the initial screening and could resettle in the United States. The passage does not say what birth date was recorded for Omar. Omar writes that the family passed health screenings and received vaccinations before leaving for the United States. Catholic Charities arranged for them to live in Arlington, Virginia, and the family traveled to Nairobi for a pre-departure orientation. Omar describes being disappointed by what she initially saw in America compared with the image presented to refugees before their arrival. She recounted a conversation she had with her father following their arrival to the country, "This isn't America," Omar said. Her father responded: "This isn't our America. We'll get to our America." In Arlington, all seven family members moved into a two-bedroom apartment and applied for Social Security cards, according to the memoir. Omar and her siblings underwent another medical screening and received the same immunizations they had received in Kenya because they needed medical records to attend school. Omar writes that her father protested because he worried the additional shots could make them sick. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Edward T. somalia.summary: U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar's memoir, *This Is What America Looks Like: My Journey From Refugee to Congresswoman*, recounts her early life, including her family's escape from Somalia's civil war and their resettlement in the United States. Omar describes her childhood in Mogadishu, the journey through Kenya, and the refugee screening process that led to their immigration. The memoir has faced scrutiny, particularly regarding her birth date and allegations surrounding her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, which Omar has consistently denied. Critics have questioned her age based on her accounts of the civil war, but her memoir aligns with her publicly listed birth date of October 4, 1982. Omar reflects on the challenges of adapting to life in America and the misconceptions surrounding her identity. Despite facing allegations of immigration fraud, no legal findings have substantiated these claims. Omar's narrative emphasizes resilience and the complexities of her journey as a refugee turned congresswoman.

Topics Charities About Our Office News & Information File a Complaint Order Publications Contact Us Search Our Site Attorney General Ellison again leads court defense of Temporary Protected Status for immigrants from Somalia Leads coalition of 17 AGs in amicus brief asking federal court to hear appeal; second time this year AG Ellison and coalition have supported TPS for Somali Americans October 27, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — For the second time this year, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has led a coalition of 17 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief in support of a lawsuit to block Department of Homeland Security’s termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somali immigrants . The TPS program is a crucial humanitarian lifeline that Congress established in the 1990 to protect immigrants from being returned to countries like Somalia that have been deemed unsafe, allowing them to work and build a life in the United States. Approximately 3,850 immigrants from Somalia have been living in the United States with TPS or have had pending applications for TPS, many of them in Minnesota. “The Trump Administration’s insistence on terminating Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals isn’t only cruel, it’s harmful to communities across Minnesota and in every state where Somalis live, work, grow the economy, pay taxes, and give back,” Attorney General Ellison said. “I led this coalition of attorneys general supporting the plaintiffs who want to block the revocation of TPS for Somalis because we recognize the contributions of our Somali neighbors that strengthen our states and our people and do not want our states to be harmed if the revocation is allowed to stand.” This is the second amicus brief that Attorney General Ellison led this year of attorneys general defending Somali TPS , following the first one he led in April 2026 . The brief filed yesterday in African Communities Together v. Mullin supports the plaintiffs’ request that the appeals court reverse a lower court decision not to grant emergency relief and block the Department of Homeland Security’s revocation of TPS for Somali nationals. The coalition states are home to at least 53,000 Somali immigrants, with Minnesota alone home to at least 37,500. These numbers include TPS holders, whom the coalition states have taken public steps to support because Somali immigrants, including TPS holders, make vital contributions to the communities in which they live: they are valued neighbors, homeowners, coworkers, teachers, students, entrepreneurs, caregivers, construction workers, union members, and parents. Stripping TPS holders of legal status would harm the residents, economies, and public health and safety of Minnesota and the coalition states. In the brief , Attorney General Ellison and the coalition highlight the harms Minnesota and the coalition states and their residents — including the U.S. citizen children of Somali nationals with TPS — will experience with the revocation of TPS for Somalis, arguing that it would harm their states’ economies, residents, and public health and safety. Somali immigrants make a significant, positive impact on Minnesota’s economy: their annual economic impact is roughly $8.6 billion and they pay an estimated $228 million annually in state and local taxes. They also contribute to critical industries: as of 2019, over 15 percent of all Somali immigrants in Minnesota worked in home health care, and Somali workers made up 11 percent of the state’s workers in animal food processing. Somali immigrants are also known for their entrepreneurship, starting businesses that create jobs, circulate dollars locally, and revitalize communities. The Minnesota Department of Economic Development has recognized that “[w]ithout foreign-born workers,” of which Somalis are the second-largest group in Minnesota, “many businesses in Minnesota would not have the workers they need to operate, let alone grow and thrive.” Allowing the revocation of Somalia’s TPS designation to stand endangers these economic contributions to communities in every corner of Minnesota. Creating new undocumented citizens by revoking TPS for Somali nationals would have ripple effects throughout educational and public-health systems. Operation Metro Surge, the purpose of which President Trump claimed was to root out fraud in Somali communities in Minnesota, led to high rates of absenteeism throughout public schools in Minneapolis, including of U.S. citizen children of Somali immigrants — many of whom themselves are U.S. citizens. Stripping legal status from Somali immigrants also risks serious negative consequences for public health. Everyone benefits when residents are vaccinated or seek testing and treatment for infectious diseases. But undocumented immigrants are often reluctant to seek medical treatment due to fear of detention and deportation. Newly undocumented former TPS holders may also not seek treatment for their U.S. citizen children. Children of undocumented immigrants frequently miss preventive annual exams and are often sicker when seeking emergency room care. In Minneapolis, 40 percent of respondents to a recent survey who needed to go to urgent care or the hospital during Operation Metro Surge reported they stayed home because of fears about ICE agents, and 30 percent of respondents who had a regularly scheduled vaccine during the operation missed the vaccine out of the same fears. The impacts on the mental health and well-being of revoking TPS for Somali nationals on their U.S. citizen children would also be severe. Children of undocumented parents in the United States frequently experience persistent anxiety from fear that a family member may be deported. During Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, immigration officers targeted individuals they believed appeared to be Somali regardless of citizenship or immigration status, demonstrating that these fears were unfortunately well founded. Mental health consequences are even more severe when these fears are realized and families are forcibly separated. Parental deportation is deeply traumatic for children and is linked to extreme psychological distress, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, externalizing behaviors such as aggression, and difficulties sleeping. In the brief, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition note that revoking Somalia’s TPS designation would present current TPS holders, particularly those with U.S. citizen children, with an agonizing choice: return to Somalia alone, leaving their children behind; taking their U.S. citizen children with them to a dangerous country that the children do not know; or staying in the United States without authorization and living with significant fear and uncertainty, knowing they cannot work legally and could be forcibly removed to Somalia at any time. History of TPS for Somali nationals Somalia was first designated for TPS in 1991 by Acting Attorney General William Barr due to “extraordinary and temporary conditions.” Civil war has raged in Somalia for the ensuing 35 years, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths, children being forced into combat, extrajudicial killings, sexual and gender-based violence, and other human-rights abuses. Given the ongoing violence and suffering, Somalia’s TPS designation had been continually in place until now. In November 2025, President Trump posted on social media that he was “hereby terminating, effective immediately, the Temporary Protected Status (TPS Program) for Somalis in Minnesota...” Since then, President Trump has repeatedly launched racist attacks against Somali immigrants, calling them “garbage” and “stupid people” with “low IQs” “from a crooked country, disgusting country, one of the worst countries in the world.” In January 2026, Kristi then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced she was terminating Somalia’s TPS designation in part even though she did not claim that Somalia as a whole is safe and despite the fact that the U.S. State Department has issued its highest travel advisory for Somalia , warning travelers, “Do not travel to Somalia for any reason,” because of “unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism,” and more. Following a June 2026 decision of the U.S. Supreme Court, DHS revoked TPS for immigrants from Somalia on August 14, 2026. Attorney General Ellison led the coalition that filed the amicus brief . Joining Attorney General Ellison in the coalition are the attorneys general of California, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Vermont, and Washington.
